cards.claim: Candidate explicitly reframes the prompt — rather than building an assessment tool, scopes to a concrete enterprise pain point (client onboarding intake) with stated reasons tied to the job description's actual criteria.

citation.quote: The brief asks for something that evaluates AI Builder candidates well. I considered building an assessment tool, but I kept returning to what the job description actually rewards: finding a real pain point inside an ambiguous enterprise context and shipping a workflow that respects governance.

refutation.rationale: The quote is present verbatim in a-writeup and the surrounding context confirms the reframing rationale is explicitly tied to the job description criteria. No contradicting passage found.

cards.claim: Candidate quantifies the pain point with specific stakeholder data (25–40 minutes per client re-keying) and names the downstream failure modes (billing and conflict-check errors) to justify where AI adds tangible value.

citation.quote: Coordinators told me the re-keying alone takes 25 to 40 minutes per client and errors surface weeks later as billing and conflict-check problems. The workflow is repetitive, rule-bound, and full of judgment calls at the edges — exactly the shape where an agent helps with the middle and humans must own the edges.

refutation.rationale: The specific figures (25–40 minutes) and downstream failure modes (billing and conflict-check problems) appear verbatim in a-writeup and are self-consistent with the rest of the document. No contradicting passage found.

cards.claim: Candidate names three explicit out-of-scope domains (conflict checks, fee arrangements, ledger writes) with stated reasons, demonstrating a reasoned choice about where AI should not operate.

citation.quote: The agent owns parsing, extraction, formatting, and notification. It does not own conflict checks (regulated judgment), fee arrangements (commercial judgment), or anything that writes to the ledger. Those stay human, and the workflow is built so they cannot be reached from the automated path.

refutation.rationale: All three out-of-scope domains and their stated reasons are present verbatim in a-writeup, and the claim of structural exclusion is reinforced by the workflow's connection map, which shows no edges to any conflict-check or fee-arrangement node.

cards.claim: Workflow places an explicit human review gate on every extracted client profile before it enters the CRM, with a stated rationale distinguishing the extraction artifact from the record of truth.

citation.quote: A human reviews every extracted client profile before it enters the CRM — extraction is allowed to be wrong; the record of truth is not.

refutation.rationale: The write-up describes the human review gate in the quoted sentence, but the workflow export's connection map shows 'Validate required fields' connecting directly to 'Create CRM record' with no intervening human-approval node — the structural artifact does not demonstrate the gate the write-up describes.

cards.claim: Workflow structurally prevents the automated path from reaching regulated steps (conflict checks, fee arrangements, ledger writes), making autonomy limits architectural rather than prompt-based.

citation.quote: I think the most important design skill in agentic work is deciding what the agent must never do, and making that structural rather than aspirational.

refutation.rationale: The write-up asserts the autonomy limits are structural, but the workflow export contains no nodes for conflict checks, fee arrangements, or ledger writes at all — their absence from the export means the claim of structural prevention cannot be verified from the artifact; absence of a node is not the same as an architectural block.

cards.claim: The workflow export shows a branching validation node that routes failing records to a dedicated exceptions channel with original documents attached, providing an explicit failure path rather than silent loss.

refutation.rationale: The exceptions Slack node exists in the export and the quote is accurate, but the workflow's connection map shows no edge from 'Exceptions: route to review' to any document-attachment step, and the 'Daily exceptions digest' schedule trigger node has no outbound connections at all — the claimed cap-and-digest logic and original-document attachment are described in text but not wired in the export.

cards.claim: Demo transcript confirms that the out-of-scope steps (conflict checks, fee arrangements) are unreachable from the automated path, not merely instructed away.

citation.quote: The parts I didn't automate — conflict checks and fee arrangements — aren't reachable from this path at all, which I think matters more than any prompt instruction.

refutation.rationale: The transcript quote supports the claim as stated, but 'unreachable from this path' is the candidate's assertion during a narrated demo rather than a structural demonstration — the workflow export has no conflict-check node to be blocked, so the claim rests entirely on say-so rather than observable architecture.

cards.claim: Candidate ships a complete, runnable n8n workflow export covering the full pipeline from webhook trigger through attachment parsing, Claude extraction, field validation, CRM record creation, Slack notification, and exceptions routing.

citation.quote: "name": "Client Onboarding Triage", "nodes": [ { "name": "Intake form received", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.webhook" ... "Parse attachments" ... "Extract client profile (Claude)" ... "Validate required fields" ... "Create CRM record" ... "Notify onboarding channel" ... "Exceptions: route to review"

refutation.rationale: All seven named node types (webhook, parse attachments, Claude extraction, validate fields, CRM record, Slack notification, exceptions routing) are present in the workflow export with matching node names, and the quote accurately represents the node list.

cards.claim: Demo transcript shows the workflow executing end-to-end on a real synthetic fixture, including webhook firing, Claude extraction returning structured JSON, CRM record creation, and Slack notification.

citation.quote: The webhook fires, attachments get parsed, and here's the Claude extraction node returning the structured profile. Notice jurisdiction came back as Ontario and entity type as corporation — both correct for this fixture.

refutation.rationale: The transcript quote shows the webhook firing, Claude returning structured JSON with specific correct values (Ontario, corporation), CRM record creation, and Slack notification — all steps described in the claim are visible in the narrated demo excerpt.

cards.claim: Extraction prompt in the workflow is specific and reusable: it names the target fields, specifies JSON-only output format, and includes a no-guessing instruction for missing fields.

citation.quote: "prompt": "Extract a structured client profile from the intake text: legal_name, jurisdiction, entity_type, engagement_type, key_contacts[]. Return JSON only. If a required field is missing, set it to null — do not guess."

refutation.rationale: The prompt text is present verbatim in a-workflow node id 3, names all target fields, specifies JSON-only output, and includes the null/no-guessing instruction. The quote accurately represents the artifact.

cards.claim: Candidate tested all twenty synthetic profiles across happy path and both exception paths before recording the demo, with two profiles deliberately malformed to exercise failure handling.

citation.quote: the demo runs entirely on twenty synthetic client profiles I authored by hand — two of them deliberately malformed (a missing jurisdiction, a contact block pasted as an image description) to exercise the exception path. In a real deployment the extraction call would run inside the firm's approved environment, not a public endpoint, and the intake bucket would carry the same retention policy as the matter file. I tested the happy path and both exception paths against all twenty profiles before recording the demo.

refutation.rationale: The twenty-profile test and both exception paths are claimed in the write-up but are not verifiable from the demo transcript (which shows only one happy-path and one malformed fixture) or the workflow export; this rests entirely on the candidate's assertion.

cards.claim: Demo transcript shows the malformed fixture executing its exception path live: null jurisdiction triggers validation failure and routes to exceptions channel with original documents attached.

citation.quote: I'll submit the malformed fixture with no jurisdiction. Extraction returns null for jurisdiction because the prompt forbids guessing, validation fails it, and it lands in the exceptions channel with the original documents attached. Nothing silently disappears.

refutation.rationale: The transcript quote explicitly narrates the null-jurisdiction fixture triggering validation failure and routing to the exceptions channel with original documents attached, matching the claim step for step.

cards.claim: Candidate identifies a specific named failure mode (confidently wrong legal name from the extraction model) and traces it back to the design decision that mitigates it (the human review gate).

citation.quote: The extraction model will eventually produce a confidently wrong legal name; the review step exists for exactly that day.

refutation.rationale: The write-up names the specific failure mode (confidently wrong legal name) and directly connects it to the human review gate as the mitigation; both elements are present in the quoted passage and consistent with the broader document.

cards.claim: Demo runs on hand-authored synthetic PII data rather than real client data, with the production data handling approach described as running inside the firm's approved environment.

citation.quote: Intake documents contain client PII, so the demo runs entirely on twenty synthetic client profiles I authored by hand — two of them deliberately malformed (a missing jurisdiction, a contact block pasted as an image description) to exercise the exception path. In a real deployment the extraction call would run inside the firm's approved environment, not a public endpoint.

refutation.rationale: The write-up explicitly states the PII rationale, names twenty synthetic profiles authored by hand, and describes the production data handling approach; the claim accurately reflects what is described, and the substance grade is 'described' — appropriate given this is not demonstrated in the export.

cards.claim: Regulated judgment steps (conflict checks) are excluded from automation on principle and made structurally unreachable, treating governance as a load-bearing design constraint.

citation.quote: No automatic conflict screening — that is a regulated judgment I will not automate on principle.

refutation.rationale: The write-up quote supports exclusion on principle, but the 'structurally unreachable' portion of the claim is not demonstrated by the workflow export, which simply omits any conflict-check node rather than containing an architectural barrier preventing its invocation.

cards.claim: Exception routing design caps per-run exception noise at two and routes the remainder to a daily digest, explicitly treating adoption risk and coordinator trust as a safety-relevant design variable.

citation.quote: adoption risk is real: if the exceptions channel gets noisy, coordinators will stop trusting it — so I capped exceptions at two per run and route the rest to a daily digest instead.

refutation.rationale: The write-up describes capping exceptions at two per run and routing the rest to a daily digest, but the workflow export's connections map shows the 'Daily exceptions digest' schedule trigger node has no outbound connections and is not wired into the exceptions path at all — the described cap-and-digest mechanism does not exist in the artifact.

cards.claim: Candidate provides a prioritised cut list with explicit reasons for each omission: OCR (timebox), conflict screening (regulatory principle), fine-tuning/vector store (variation handled by prompt).

citation.quote: No OCR for scanned PDFs — the intake form already produces text, and OCR quality problems would have eaten the timebox. No automatic conflict screening — that is a regulated judgment I will not automate on principle. No fine-tuning, no vector store: the extraction prompt plus validation rules handle the variation I could test.

refutation.rationale: All three cut items (OCR, conflict screening, fine-tuning/vector store) appear in the write-up with explicit stated reasons matching the claim; the substance grade is 'described' and the quote accurately represents the passage.

cards.claim: Candidate names a concrete residual risk conceding a real weakness: the workflow currently over-trusts the intake form's entity type claim.

citation.quote: The workflow currently trusts the intake form's claim about entity type more than it should.

refutation.rationale: The specific weakness (over-trusting the intake form's entity type claim) is named verbatim in the write-up under 'Risks I'd flag first,' consistent with the claim.

cards.claim: Next steps named follow directly from the identified limits rather than being a general wish list: a feedback loop from coordinator corrections back into the extraction prompt, justified as the cheapest training data available.

citation.quote: With more time I would add a feedback loop from coordinator corrections back into the extraction prompt, because the corrections are the cheapest training data the firm owns.

refutation.rationale: The feedback-loop next step is explicitly tied to the identified limit (extraction errors) and justified with a concrete reason (cheapest training data), directly matching the claim that it follows from identified limits rather than being a general wish list.

paragraphs.text: The candidate's problem framing is the strongest area in the evidence set. Across three supported cards, the submission shows an explicit reframe of the prompt toward a concrete enterprise pain point, stakeholder-specific figures justifying where AI adds value, and a reasoned out-of-scope list with stated reasons for each excluded domain. All three cards are graded 'described' — the reasoning is credible and coherent in the write-up — but the framing work itself does not have a separate demonstrable artifact beyond the narrative. No cards in this competency were marked unverified or contradicted.

Builder execution is supported by the strongest direct evidence in the submission. The n8n workflow export contains all seven named node types, the extraction prompt is present verbatim with specific field targeting and a no-guessing instruction, and the demo transcript shows a live end-to-end run including a malformed fixture exercising the exception path. The extractor grades these cards 'demonstrated' and the skeptic supports them, with one caveat: ev-08 carries a citation-mismatch flag whose origin is not resolved in the record. The demo narration is specific enough (correct jurisdiction and entity type returned for the fixture) that a candidate unfamiliar with the work would struggle to reproduce it, but the panel should probe whether the export is fully self-contained and runnable without additional configuration.

The agentic workflow and handoff design evidence contains the most significant extractor–skeptic disagreements in the set. The write-up describes three design decisions — a human review gate before CRM record creation, structural prevention of regulated steps, and a cap-and-digest exception routing mechanism — but the skeptic marks all three unverified or contradicted against the workflow export. Specifically: the connection map shows 'Validate required fields' wiring directly to 'Create CRM record' with no human-approval node; the regulated steps are absent from the export rather than architecturally blocked; and the daily digest node has no outbound connections. These are material gaps between the described design and the artifact, and they are the highest-priority questions for the live interview.

Evaluation discipline and responsible AI design are each partially evidenced. On evaluation, one failure mode is demonstrated live in the demo transcript and a specific named extraction failure is connected to a mitigation, but the claim of testing all twenty profiles across both exception paths rests entirely on assertion in the write-up with no corroborating artifact. On responsible AI, the use of synthetic PII data is supported, and the principled exclusion of regulated judgment is clearly stated; however, the cap-and-digest adoption-risk mechanism — the most operationally specific responsible-AI design choice — is contradicted by the export. Communication of tradeoffs is consistently supported: the cut list is explicit, the entity-type weakness is named as a real concession, and the next-steps are tied to identified limits rather than being a general wish list.
